technical-summary:
MA20 (RV495 corrected + RV496 first half): collapsed the duplicated Pattern A family scaffolding without weakening validation.

Added FamilyPin to recipe_definitions.py: a frozen dataclass holding one family's authoritative facts (family_id, payload_contract, result_contract, supported_modes, ownership_scope_required) with a .contracts property and a .definition(provider_id) builder that synthesizes recipe_id as f'{provider_id}.{family_id}' and recipe_version '1'. The four *_family.py modules now declare a single PIN constant instead of each wrapping the same five constants in an X_definition(provider_id) factory plus a one-entry X_family_contracts() dict builder. The three pure pin modules dropped from ~38 lines to 16.

Rewrote build_automation_registry as one FamilyRegistrar table (pin, eligibility predicate, handler factory) driven by a single registration loop, replacing four copy-pasted loops and a 40-line aliased import block. A new Pattern A family now costs one table row plus a handler. Renamed generated_surface_family._make_handler to make_generated_surface_handler (it was an underscore-private name exported in __all__ and imported across modules).

IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO RV495: the review originally proposed deriving RecipeDefinition and the family contract map FROM the descriptor declaration, on the premise that register()'s VAL-9 check proved the code-side definition was a redundant copy of config. That was wrong and was NOT implemented. The code-side definition is the family's authoritative pin; the descriptor is a per-provider declaration; VAL-9 is the cross-check between them. Verified empirically: registering self-provided-lsp for pi with a descriptor declaring supported_modes ('apply','status','plan') is rejected with VAL-PREC-009 because the family pins only ('apply','status'). Had the definition been derived from the declaration, that registration would have succeeded, dispatch would have accepted mode='plan', and the handler -- which has no plan branch -- would have fallen through to its apply path and run the pi-lens installer. A config typo would have turned a planning call into a mutation. The pin therefore stays in code; only its expression was collapsed. Re-verified after the refactor that VAL-PREC-009 still rejects the same drift. RV495 has been rewritten to record the corrected design.

MA26 step 3: decision (a) DECIDED by owner -- the codex writer enables [features] codex_hooks when the owned scope is non-empty after apply, and prune never touches it (disabling a global flag we did not enable is an unowned mutation). Former decision (b) 'managed_id scheme' DISSOLVED as a non-question: ManagedFragmentRegistry is already the generic foundation 'atomic ownership registry for opaque named fragments' and mcp_ownership_registry is merely its one MCP-scoped instance, so hooks reuse it as ManagedFragmentRegistry(project_root, 'managed-hooks.json', top_level_key='providers'), recording managed_id -> the exact command string written. technical-summary:
Answered two owner design challenges with evidence, and reduced MA26's scope as a result.

RV508 -- 'are hooks just plugins in disguise?': No. An opencode plugin is a flat-array entry in .opencode/opencode.json keyed by PACKAGE NAME, at most one per name, meaning 'auto-install this package at startup' (per the adapter's own docstring). A codex hook is an event-keyed nested-list entry identified by (event, command) with MANY entries per event as the normal case. The cardinality difference is decisive: the plugin array structurally cannot hold two entries under one key, but MA26 step 5 exists precisely so our hook and a user's hook coexist on one SessionStart event. No provider has both, and none models hooks in a descriptor at all -- codex hooks.json is written directly by codex_recipe.py, bypassing the descriptor. The question did surface a real smell, but it points at plugin-entry: PluginEntryRequest carries an untyped {entry_id, options} bag (the generic blob MA20 step 4 forbids), it is the only family on PluginConfigSpec rather than ManagedConfigSpec, the only singular family with no ownership scope, and it has N=1 declaring provider so its claim to be a generic mechanic is untested.

RV509 -- 'can hooks and plugins just be removed if we use managed config?': Largely yes, for the SERVICE layer. sync_managed_config(spec, project_root, owner_scope, desired_entries, *, registry, managed_ids) already exists in foundation, is entry-type-agnostic (the desired-entry value is opaque Any), and already implements merge-owned/preserve-foreign/prune-owned-only over reconcile_fragments. MO06 already converted managed-mcp and model-projection into thin bindings over it -- their docstrings say so verbatim. plugin-entry is the ONLY family bypassing the engine, calling spec.reader/writer/remover directly, which breaks the invariant stated in managed_config.py's own docstring ('exactly two places ever touch .writer/.remover'); tests/unit/foundation/toolchains/test_managed_mutation_boundaries.py::test_direct_managed_spec_calls_are_core_or_recorded_violation already FAILS naming plugin_entries.py -- a red test I had previously mis-attributed to MO02 audit noise. PluginConfigSpec is redundant with ManagedConfigSpec: the only difference is keyed access, and the opencode plugin array is already a name-keyed collection.

MA26 scope reduced accordingly: step 3 no longer specifies a managed-hooks SERVICE. The provider side becomes (i) hooks_config ManagedConfigSpec + capability declaration in codex.yaml, (ii) a codex hooks_format adapter presenting hooks.json as a name-keyed dict (key = command, value = {event, timeout}), pairing with the ManagedFragmentRegistry managed_id -> command mapping, and (iii) a ~15-line typed binding over sync_managed_config copying services/mcp.py. Step 4 rewritten to forbid hand-rolling a service/preamble/ownership store. Step 5 downgraded to mostly a regression test, since preservation is inherited from reconcile_fragments once the engine is used -- the data-loss defect exists precisely because the current recipe bypasses it. Error prefix self-corrected PHK -> PHKS (all 12 existing provider prefixes are 4 characters).

technical-summary:
SECURITY REGRESSION FIXED, plus the planning flaw that caused it.

LEAK: redact_text had been removed from providers/services/self_provided_lsp_handler.py, so a failing pi-lens hook surfaced raw provider output into the user-facing action_needed field. Reproduced exactly: action_needed came back as 'token=sk-secret-value install failed'. Restored redact_text on both the hook-result path (_hook_outcome, covering error/stderr/stdout) and the exception path. Caught only because tests/unit/coding_lsp/test_provider_lsp_provision.py::test_self_provided_lsp_surfaces_redacted_hook_failure_detail asserts the secret is absent -- the test earned its keep.

ROOT CAUSE WAS MY OWN OU01 STEP ORDERING. The OU01 rewrite listed step 3 'remove the in-flight fan-out' BEFORE steps 4-5 'enforce at the egress boundaries' and 'close the git-managed gap'. Following that order deletes the scattered guards before their replacement exists, leaving a window with NEITHER. The in-flight redaction is a stopgap, but it must not be removed until the boundary that replaces it is built and proven. Corrected OU01 with an explicit ORDER OF WORK header (1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5 -> 3 -> 7 -> 8) and rewrote step 3 to require that steps 4-5 have landed first, that the boundary is proven to catch a planted secret BEFORE deletion and still catches it after, and that each deletion is justified by 'an enforced boundary downstream now covers this value' rather than merely 'this is in-flight'. The regression itself is recorded in the step as the reason.

Added an inline comment at the restored call site explaining that OU01 will delete it once the egress boundary exists, so it is not mistaken for scatter to be cleaned up early.

technical-summary:
Fixed a defect that blocked EVERY agent launch, found by attempting a live opencode run.

DEFECT: the installer writes .audiagentic/config/runtime/providers.yaml containing only '# Installation marker'. YAML parses that to an EMPTY MAPPING, which load_provider_config passed straight to strict schema validation, raising VAL-PCFG-001 ('contract-version' and 'providers' required) on a file the installer itself wrote. A MISSING file was handled gracefully (returns the empty default) but an existing-but-empty one was fatal, so a freshly-installed project could not launch any provider. Reproduced live: agent_llm_run against the opencode profile failed with VAL-PCFG-001 after correctly resolving provider-id=opencode and model-id=brutus/coder-quality-mid.

FIX: load_provider_config now treats a non-dict OR empty payload as the same state as a missing file and returns {'contract-version': 'v1', 'providers': {}}. Note the first attempt checked only `not isinstance(payload, dict)` and did not work, because load_yaml_file returns an empty dict rather than None for a comment-only file; the check needed `or not payload`. Also aligned load_provider_config_lenient, which had the mirror-image inconsistency: it returned the raw empty mapping rather than the default, so the strict and lenient loaders disagreed about what a freshly-installed project means. A test asserting the two agree caught that.

MODEL RENAME: agent profile deep-coder-opencode moved from brutus/deep-coder to brutus/coder-quality-mid (brutus = 10.10.100.10), description updated.
